title: Prospective Human Validation of Artificial Intelligence Interventions in Cardiology

reading.body:
Across 64 prospective cardiology studies from 2015 to 2023, 44 reported clear gains over expert clinicians, but only 11 were randomized and only 22 shared models or datasets.

The pattern is a field moving faster than its evidence. Fifty-nine of the 64 studies appeared after 2020, so the literature is young and still concentrated in narrow tasks: imaging, heart pumping function, rhythm problems, and blocked heart arteries. Convolutional neural networks on images were the most common approach. Performance against a benchmark is not the same as performance in routine care, and the small randomized share is the gap that matters most.

The transparency number is the one that constrains everything downstream. Only 22 of 64 studies released models or datasets, which means most reported results cannot be independently reproduced or audited. For AI in medicine this is not a minor omission. A claim that a model matches clinicians is only as durable as the ability of an outside group to check it, and roughly two thirds of these studies do not permit that check.

What the data does not cover is deployment. It says nothing about compute, infrastructure, or power, and nothing about cost, staffing, or what happened when these tools met real patient volumes. It also stops at December 2023, so any change in transparency or trial design since then is outside its scope. The honest reading is that cardiology AI has demonstrated narrow task competence and has not yet demonstrated that it can be verified at scale.

explain_beginner: This review examined heart care studies where artificial intelligence was tested with people and compared with doctors or accepted medical standards. From 2015 through 2023, the authors found 64 such studies. Most appeared after 2020. In 44 studies, the AI produced clear improvements in care or operations compared with expert clinicians. However, only 11 were randomized studies, and only 22 shared their models or datasets. The takeaway is that AI can perform as well as doctors on narrow tasks, but stronger testing and more openness are still needed before routine use.
explain_business: For executives, this review suggests that heart care AI is promising but not yet mature enough for broad, unchecked deployment. Across 64 studies, 44 showed clear care or workflow gains over expert clinicians, often in narrow areas such as imaging, heart pumping function, rhythm problems, and blocked heart arteries. However, only 11 were randomized controlled studies, and only 22 shared their models or datasets. Most studies were recent. The practical decision is to prioritize AI tools for specific tasks with clear boundaries, require independent validation and transparency, and invest in testing how clinicians and AI work together before scaling adoption.
explain_practitioner: The authors searched Scopus and MEDLINE for peer reviewed papers from January 2015 to December 2023 that prospectively compared AI tools in cardiology with expert or standard benchmarks. They screened 2,351 records and included 64 studies. Fifty-nine appeared after 2020, and 11 were randomized controlled studies. Forty-four reported clear care or workflow gains over expert clinicians. Common areas were imaging, heart pumping function, rhythm problems, and blocked heart arteries. The most frequent model type was a convolutional neural network, and images were the most common input. Only 22 studies shared their models or datasets. AI often matches clinicians on narrow tasks, but more randomized and actual care testing is needed.
